document_check.note: Document is Cheng X, Huang X, Yu Q, et al. 'Associations between brain structures, cognition and dual-task performance in patients with mild cognitive impairment: A study based on voxel-based morphology', Human Movement Science 97 (2024) 103257. It is a single-visit comparison of 30 MCI patients and 30 healthy controls, and within the same study it reports single-task and dual-task Timed Up and Go (TUG) times, which is the head-to-head behavioural dissociation that convergence VF-25 describes.

cited_result: Principal result supporting VF-25 (behavioural arm): dual-task TUG execution time was longer in MCI than in controls (29.23 +/- 8.02 s vs 24.92 +/- 4.42 s, t = -2.58, p = 0.012), while single-task TUG time did not differ (17.29 +/- 2.34 s vs 17.60 +/- 2.89 s, t = 0.47, p = 0.643); 30 MCI vs 30 healthy controls.
tool_reason: The cited result compares single- and dual-task TUG times between MCI patients and controls measured at one visit, which the brief assigns to the JBI analytical cross-sectional checklist. The groups are defined by current condition and compared on a concurrent measure, not on past exposures, so the case-control checklist does not fit.

domains.domain: Item 1: Criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined
domains.rationale: Explicit MCI inclusion criteria (Petersen and Albert core clinical criteria, CDR, MoCA and MMSE ranges), exclusion criteria and separate control criteria are all stated.

signalling.question: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
signalling.quote: The diagnostic criteria for MCI were the same as that outlined by Petersen et al. (Petersen, 2004). ... (4) no dementia, CDR ≤0.5, MOCA score of >18 and < 26 points, Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) ranging 24 to 27. ... The inclusion criteria for the HC group were as follows: (1) absence of cognitive impairment with an MMSE score of >28, a MOCA score ≥26; (2) absence of physical, mental, or neurological disorders; (3) normal functional activity.

domains.domain: Item 2: Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.rationale: Location, recruitment sources and demographics are given, but there is no recruitment period, no count of people screened, and nothing on which recruitment source (clinic or community) supplied each group. That last point matters for whether the two groups are comparable.

signalling.question: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
signalling.quote: The participants were recruited from the Department of Rehabilitation Medicine Clinic, the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, and the community through recruitment announcement. ... We enrolled 30 patients with MCI and 30 healthy controls (HCs) aged 50 or above, and they were all right-handed. (Looked for: recruitment dates, numbers screened, source of each group; none reported.)

domains.domain: Item 3: Exposure (MCI group status) measured in a valid and reliable way
domains.rationale: The measure that defines the groups (MoCA) was a culturally adapted version, and one trained therapist administered it to every participant under a set protocol. Who applied the CDR and the clinical criteria is not stated, but the instrument that carries the group assignment was used consistently.

signalling.question: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: All participants underwent a cognitive assessment using the Chinese version of the MoCA, which considers cultural and linguistical differences (Tu et al., 2013). ... All participants were evaluated by the same therapist who had been strictly trained to follow the required protocol.

domains.domain: Item 4: Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition
domains.rationale: MCI was defined by published core clinical criteria with numeric screening thresholds. Note: 'objective evidence of cognitive impairment' is not operationalised beyond the MoCA and MMSE ranges.

signalling.question: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
signalling.quote: The inclusion criteria for MCI patients refers to the core clinical diagnostic criteria and other studies (Albert et al., 2011; Leandri et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2021): (1) presence of subjective memory complaints or informant-reported cognitive complaints; (2) presence of objective evidence of cognitive impairment; (3) preserved functional abilities or normal activities of daily living

domains.rationale: The authors measured and compared age, sex, BMI and education between groups, and they excluded comorbidities and medications likely to affect gait or cognition.

signalling.question: Were confounding factors identified?
signalling.quote: There were no significant differences in sex, age, body mass index, or years of education between the two groups (p > 0.05) (Table 1). [Exclusion criteria:] (2) taking medicines which may improve or impair cognitive performance; (3) self-reported or physician-diagnosis of severe peripheral neuropathy, lower-extremity arthritis, and visual or hearing abnormalities

domains.domain: Item 6: Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated
domains.rationale: The groups were not matched, stratified or adjusted. TUG times were compared with unadjusted independent-sample t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, and the only covariate adjustment in the paper is TIV in the grey-matter models. Excluding comorbidities is a partial design-level restriction, but it does not deal with education (10.13 vs 11.53 years, p = 0.097) or sex (4/26 vs 7/23 male/female), both plausibly relevant to the phone-dialling dual task. The null single-task result makes purely motor confounding less likely, but it is not a stated strategy.

signalling.question: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
signalling.quote: The data normally distributed were compared based on independent-sample t-tests between groups. The data which was not normally distributed were explored using the nonparametric test (Mann-Whitney U). (Looked for: matching, stratification or multivariable adjustment of the TUG comparison; none reported. Covariate adjustment appears only for GMV: 'SPM-based regression models adjusted for TIV'.)

domains.domain: Item 7: Outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way
domains.rationale: The TUG task and its dual-task version are described and cited to a prior protocol, but it is a modified task (10 m walk, phone retrieval, 11-digit dialling). The paper does not say who timed it, whether the timer was blind to group, what timing device was used, how many trials were run, or whether it is reliable. Dual-task time also includes the time needed to finish dialling.

signalling.question: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: During the single-task condition, participants were asked to rise from a chair, walk at usual pace to a table 10 m away and retrieve a cellphone, then return back to the starting point and sit down. In the dual-task condition, after they got the cellphone, participants were taught to dial a series of numbers in 11 digits on a card during walking back. The total time taken to complete the entire task (finishing dialing and sitting back on the chair) was recorded. (Looked for: assessor identity and blinding, timing method, number of trials, reliability; none reported.)

domains.rationale: The between-group tests (t-test or Mann-Whitney chosen by distribution) suit each two-group comparison, and the reported t statistics agree with the means and SDs. Caveat: the dissociation is inferred from one significant and one non-significant test. No group-by-task interaction or dual-task cost was tested, and 30 per group gives limited power to support the single-task null.

signalling.question: Was appropriate statistical analysis used?
signalling.quote: There was no significant difference in the single task execution time between the MCI and HC groups (MCI: 17.29 ± 2.34 s, HC: 17.60 ± 2.89 s, t = 0.47, p = 0.643). However, a significant difference in the execution time of the dual-task paradigm was observed between the two groups (MCI: 29.23 ± 8.02 s, HC: 24.92 ± 4.42 s, t = −2.58, p = 0.012).

overall: High risk of bias (JBI analytical cross-sectional: item 6 No; items 2 and 7 Unclear; items 1, 3, 4, 5 and 8 Yes).
overall_rationale: By this review's rule, a 'No' on the confounder-strategy item gives high risk. The MCI-control difference in dual-task TUG time is unadjusted and the groups were not matched, so residual differences in education and sex could contribute to a dual-task effect that depends on digit dialling. It is also unclear whether the timed outcome was measured blind or reliably. The null single-task comparison partly guards against motor confounding, but the paper does not use it as a strategy.

applicability.rationale: Single hospital and community sample in Guangzhou, aged 50+ (mean about 60), mostly women (26/30 MCI). Controls were required to score MMSE > 28 and MoCA >= 26, leaving a gap against MCI's MMSE 24-27. This extreme-group design is less representative of routine differential diagnosis.
A modified TUG (10 m walk, phone retrieval, 11-digit dialling on return) rather than the standard 3 m TUG, so the dual-task times may not carry over to other dual-task protocols.
